function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written them based on the typical structure of a minimal Node.js project (an `app.js` that listens on a port, a `package.json`, etc.).  
If your repo differs, just tweak the paths or ports accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# File: Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – choose the newest LTS you prefer
FROM node:18-slim

# Maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is a small, production‑ready image.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The container listens on port **3000** – change it if your app uses another port.

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or split into separate files if you prefer).

```yaml
# File: k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use Docker Hub
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a Service on port 80.  
> * Uses `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` as the image – adjust the registry/tag if you push elsewhere.

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# File: .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image from the root `Dockerfile`.  
> * Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets needed.

---

## 4️⃣ Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# 3. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### 🎉 Done!

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically build and publish your Docker image.  
The Kubernetes manifests are ready to be applied with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image registry, or environment variables to match your production needs. Happy coding!
